questions.stem: The Italian monk who first published a description of the double entry system in 1494 was
questions.explanation: Luca Pacioli described double entry book-keeping in his book "Summa" published in Venice in 1494.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the final stage in the accounting process?
options: Recording transactions in books of original entry
questions.explanation: The process moves from recording and classifying to summarising, then to analysis, interpretation and communication.

questions.stem: Which of the following users of accounting information is mainly interested in whether a business can pay its debts as they fall due?
questions.explanation: Creditors want to know about liquidity and the ability of the business to pay what it owes.

questions.stem: Book-keeping differs from accounting in that book-keeping
options: is concerned mainly with recording financial transactions, while accounting includes summarising, analysing and interpreting them.
is done only at the end of the year.
questions.explanation: Book-keeping is the recording stage; accounting is broader.

questions.stem: The qualitative characteristic which requires that accounting information should be free from material error and bias is
questions.explanation: Reliable information faithfully represents what it purports to represent, without material error or bias.

questions.stem: The body established by law to set and enforce financial reporting standards in Nigeria is the
questions.explanation: The FRCN, established by the Financial Reporting Council of Nigeria Act 2011, sets and enforces accounting and financial reporting standards.

questions.stem: Which of the following professional bodies is chartered to regulate the accountancy profession in Nigeria?
options: The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria
The Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria (ICAN)
questions.explanation: ICAN (established 1965) and ANAN are the statutory professional accountancy bodies in Nigeria.

questions.stem: Accounting information is said to be comparable when
options: it is presented in simple language.
it is prepared quickly after the year end.
it is audited by a chartered accountant.
users can compare it over time and with that of other entities because similar methods are used.
questions.explanation: Comparability requires consistent treatment and disclosure of policies so that trends and entities can be compared.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: The accounting equation is
questions.explanation: Every asset is financed either by the owner (capital) or by outsiders (liabilities).

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: A business has total assets of ₦850,000 and liabilities of ₦230,000. Its capital is
questions.explanation: Capital = Assets - Liabilities = 850,000 - 230,000 = ₦620,000.

questions.explanation: Assets = cash 500,000 + inventory 120,000 = ₦620,000; liabilities rise by 120,000 and capital stays at 500,000.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: Credit purchases of goods for resale are first recorded in the
questions.explanation: Credit purchases of trading goods are entered in the purchases day book before posting to the ledger.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: The source document for recording a credit sale is the
questions.explanation: The invoice issued to the customer is the source document for the sales day book.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles

questions.explanation: Under the imprest system, the amount spent is reimbursed to restore the float to ₦50,000.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles

questions.explanation: Treating capital expenditure as revenue expenditure (wrong class of account) is an error of principle.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: Which of the following errors will NOT affect the agreement of the trial balance?
options: Rent of ₦20,000 debited twice in rent account
Credit sales of ₦45,000 to Musa posted to Moses' account
A debit balance of ₦8,000 omitted from the trial balance
questions.explanation: Posting to the wrong personal account of the same class is an error of commission; debits still equal credits.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: The debit side of a trial balance totals ₦2,456,000 and the credit side ₦2,438,000. To make it agree, a suspense account will be opened with
questions.explanation: The credit side is short by 2,456,000 - 2,438,000 = ₦18,000, so suspense is credited with ₦18,000.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: The sales day book was undercast by ₦5,000, and a suspense account was opened. The correcting entry is
questions.explanation: Sales were credited ₦5,000 too little, while debtors' accounts were correct; sales is credited and suspense debited.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: In a three-column cash book, ₦80,000 cash paid into the bank is recorded as
options: debit cash column, credit bank column.
debit bank column, credit cash column (a contra entry).
debit bank column, credit capital account.
questions.explanation: Both sides are in the cash book: the bank column receives, the cash column gives.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: A credit balance on the bank column of a cash book means that the business
options: has an overdraft at the bank.
questions.explanation: Payments out of the bank exceed lodgements, so the business owes the bank.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: The cash book of a business shows a debit bank balance of ₦145,000. Cheques of ₦32,000 issued have not yet been presented, and a lodgement of ₦18,500 has not been credited by the bank. The balance on the bank statement is

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: Bank charges of ₦3,500 appear on the bank statement but not in the cash book. The cash book is updated by
options: debiting the bank column and crediting bank charges account.
adding ₦3,500 to the bank statement balance.
crediting the bank column and debiting bank charges account.
no entry, since the bank has made an error.
questions.explanation: Charges reduce the bank balance, so the cash book is credited and an expense account debited.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: Goods costing ₦15,000 taken by the owner for personal use should be recorded by
questions.explanation: Drawings increase and the cost of goods available for sale (purchases) is reduced.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: Premises, motor vehicles and machinery accounts are classified as
questions.explanation: Real accounts record assets; nominal accounts record income and expenses; personal accounts relate to persons.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: Goods returned by customers are recorded in the
questions.explanation: Returns inwards are goods sent back by customers; returns outwards are goods sent back to suppliers.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: The journal proper is used for recording
options: the purchase of fixed assets on credit and the correction of errors.
questions.explanation: Transactions that do not belong in other books of original entry, such as opening entries, corrections and credit purchases of fixed assets, go through the journal.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: In a cash book, discount allowed of ₦2,400 is recorded in the discount column on the debit side. At the end of the month the total is posted to the
questions.explanation: The memorandum column total is debited to discount allowed (an expense); the individual amounts are credited to debtors' accounts.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: Which of the following errors will be revealed by the trial balance?
options: Purchases of ₦62,000 posted to the purchases account as ₦26,000, with the creditor's account correctly credited
A credit purchase of ₦20,000 completely omitted from the books
Both debit and credit entries recorded as ₦13,000 instead of ₦31,000
Rent paid debited to the rates account
questions.explanation: A one-sided transposition makes debits differ from credits; the others leave the trial balance in agreement.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem: A business pays its electricity bill directly through a direct debit, which appears on the bank statement only. In preparing the bank reconciliation, the accountant should first
options: debit the cash book with the amount.
update the cash book by crediting it with the amount.
add the amount to the bank statement balance.
ignore it because it is the bank's error.
questions.explanation: Items on the statement but not in the cash book are entered in the cash book before reconciling.

questions.stem: The concept which assumes that a business will continue in operation for the foreseeable future is the
questions.explanation: Going concern justifies valuing assets at cost less depreciation instead of at break-up values.

questions.stem: The concept which treats the business as separate from its owner is the
questions.explanation: Under the entity concept, only the business's transactions are recorded; the owner's private affairs are excluded.

questions.stem: The concept that requires revenue and expenses to be recognised in the period in which they are earned or incurred, not when cash is received or paid, is the
questions.explanation: Accruals match income with related expenses of the same period.

questions.stem: Valuing closing inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value is an application of the
questions.explanation: Prudence avoids overstating assets and profit by anticipating losses but not gains.

questions.stem: The concept which states that every transaction has two aspects, a debit and a credit, is the
questions.explanation: Duality underlies double entry and the accounting equation.

questions.stem: A firm charges a stapler costing ₦4,500 to office expenses instead of treating it as a non-current asset. This is justified by the
questions.explanation: Items too small to influence users' decisions need not be capitalised and depreciated.

questions.stem: A business changes its depreciation method every year to show higher profits. This violates the
questions.explanation: Methods should be applied consistently from one period to another, so that results are comparable.

questions.stem: The concept which states that only transactions that can be expressed in monetary terms are recorded is the
questions.explanation: Non-monetary facts, such as staff morale, are not recorded.

questions.stem: Under the realisation concept, revenue from a credit sale is recognised when
options: the goods are delivered and the customer becomes liable to pay.
cash is received from the customer.
the order is received from the customer.
questions.explanation: Revenue is realised when goods pass to the customer and a legal obligation to pay arises.

questions.stem: A limitation of the historical cost concept is that
options: it makes accounts difficult to verify.
it requires frequent revaluation of all assets.
it records assets at their selling prices.
asset values in the statement of financial position may not reflect current values during inflation.
questions.explanation: In inflation, cost-based values become outdated and profits may be overstated.

questions.topic: The Final Accounts of a Sole Trader/Proprietorship
questions.stem: Carriage inwards is treated in the final accounts as
options: an expense in the profit and loss account.
an addition to the cost of purchases in the trading account.
questions.explanation: Carriage inwards is part of the cost of bringing goods to their present location.

questions.topic: The Final Accounts of a Sole Trader/Proprietorship
questions.stem: Carriage outwards is shown in the
options: trading account as part of cost of sales.
statement of financial position as a liability.
trading account as a deduction from sales.
profit and loss account as an expense.
questions.explanation: Carriage outwards is a distribution (selling) expense.

questions.topic: The Final Accounts of a Sole Trader/Proprietorship

questions.topic: The Final Accounts of a Sole Trader/Proprietorship
questions.stem: On 1 January 2025 a firm paid ₦96,000 insurance covering 16 months. The firm's year ends on 31 December 2025. The insurance expense for the year is
questions.explanation: Monthly cost = 96,000 / 16 = 6,000; 12 months = ₦72,000; ₦24,000 is prepaid.

questions.topic: The Final Accounts of a Sole Trader/Proprietorship

questions.explanation: Accrued expenses are amounts the business owes, so they are current liabilities.

questions.stem: Prepaid expenses are shown in the statement of financial position as
questions.explanation: Payments in advance give the business a benefit still to be received, so they are current assets.

questions.explanation: The business still owes the tenant the use of the property, so it is a liability.

questions.topic: The Final Accounts of a Sole Trader/Proprietorship
questions.stem: Commission receivable for the year was ₦60,000, but only ₦45,000 had been received by the year end. The amount credited to the income statement and the amount in the statement of financial position are respectively
questions.explanation: Income earned (₦60,000) is credited; the ₦15,000 still receivable is an accrued income (current asset).

questions.topic: The Final Accounts of a Sole Trader/Proprietorship
questions.stem: When preparing the trading account of Musa Stores, which of the following items would the accountant leave out?
options: Salaries and wages of office staff
questions.explanation: Office salaries are an operating expense in the profit and loss section.

questions.topic: The Final Accounts of a Sole Trader/Proprietorship
questions.stem: A trader's sales were ₦1,200,000 and she earns a gross margin of 25% on sales. Opening inventory was ₦150,000 and purchases were ₦930,000. Her closing inventory is

questions.topic: The Final Accounts of a Sole Trader/Proprietorship
questions.stem: Goods costing ₦25,000 taken by the owner during the year were not recorded. When preparing the final accounts, the adjustment will
options: increase purchases and reduce drawings by ₦25,000.
reduce purchases by ₦25,000 and increase drawings by ₦25,000.
questions.explanation: The goods withdrawn are not available for sale, so purchases fall and drawings rise.

questions.topic: The Final Accounts of a Sole Trader/Proprietorship
questions.stem: Closing inventory appears in the trading account and also in the statement of financial position as
questions.explanation: Inventory held at the year end will be sold in the next period, so it is a current asset.

questions.topic: The Final Accounts of a Sole Trader/Proprietorship
questions.stem: Net current assets are calculated as
questions.explanation: Net current assets (working capital) = current assets - current liabilities.

questions.explanation: Items such as loose tools are numerous and of small value, so they are valued at each year end.

questions.stem: A decrease in the allowance for doubtful debts is treated in the income statement as
options: an addition to cost of sales.
questions.explanation: Reducing the allowance releases part of earlier charges back to profit.

questions.stem: During the year bad debts of ₦12,000 were written off. Year-end receivables (after write-off) were ₦600,000 and the allowance for doubtful debts is to be kept at 4%. The opening allowance was ₦28,000. The total charge for bad and doubtful debts in the income statement is
questions.explanation: New allowance = 24,000, a decrease of 4,000; net charge = 12,000 - 4,000 = ₦8,000.

questions.stem: Trade receivables are ₦500,000. An allowance for doubtful debts of 5% is made, and then an allowance for discounts of 2% on the remaining receivables. The allowance for discounts is
The main reason for charging depreciation is to
options: raise money to buy a new asset.
spread the cost of a non-current asset over its useful life.
increase the value of the asset.
questions.explanation: Depreciation matches the cost of using the asset with the revenue it helps to earn.

questions.stem: A machine that cost ₦900,000 with accumulated depreciation of ₦540,000 was sold for ₦300,000. The result of the disposal is
questions.explanation: Net book value = 360,000; proceeds 300,000; loss = ₦60,000.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a capital reserve?
questions.explanation: Capital reserves (share premium, revaluation reserve) are not available for cash dividends; revenue reserves come from trading profits.

questions.stem: A provision differs from a reserve in that a provision is
options: an appropriation of profit set aside for future expansion.
always shown as part of shareholders' funds.
a charge against profit for a known liability or loss whose amount cannot be determined with certainty.
questions.explanation: Provisions are charges against profit; reserves are appropriations of profit.

questions.stem: A machine costing ₦1,200,000 was bought on 1 April 2025. Depreciation is 10% per annum on cost on a time basis. The depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 2025 is
Which of the following is a revenue reserve?
questions.explanation: General reserves are created out of trading profits and are revenue reserves.

questions.stem: The purpose of a manufacturing account is to determine the
options: cost of goods produced during the period.
questions.explanation: The manufacturing account shows prime cost, overheads and the cost of production.

questions.stem: Prime cost is the total of
options: direct labour and factory overheads only.
direct materials, direct labour and direct expenses.
cost of sales and selling expenses.
questions.explanation: Prime cost includes only direct costs of production.

questions.stem: Royalties paid to the owner of a patent for each unit produced are classified as
questions.explanation: Royalties vary directly with output and are part of prime cost.

questions.stem: Wages of a factory supervisor are classified as
questions.explanation: Supervisors do not work directly on the product, so their pay is an indirect factory cost.

questions.stem: Opening raw materials ₦60,000; purchases of raw materials ₦480,000; carriage on raw materials ₦15,000; closing raw materials ₦75,000; direct wages ₦350,000; royalties ₦40,000. Prime cost is

questions.explanation: Transfer value = 1,060,000 x 1.2 = 1,272,000; factory profit = ₦212,000.

questions.stem: Closing inventory of finished goods is valued at the transfer price of ₦120,000, which includes a factory profit of 20% on cost. The provision for unrealised profit is
Rent of ₦600,000 is shared between factory and office in the ratio of floor area, 3 : 1. The amount charged to the manufacturing account is
Opening raw materials ₦32,000; purchases ₦410,000; returns outwards ₦12,000; closing raw materials ₦45,000. Raw materials consumed are
The adjustment for work in progress is made in the
questions.explanation: Opening WIP is added and closing WIP deducted in arriving at cost of production.

questions.stem: Salaries of sales representatives of a manufacturing company are charged to the
questions.explanation: Selling and distribution expenses are not part of production cost.

questions.stem: In a manufacturing business, which of the following will appear in the statement of financial position as current assets?
options: Prime cost and cost of production
Raw materials, work in progress and finished goods inventory
Royalties and carriage on raw materials
questions.explanation: All three types of closing inventory are current assets.

questions.stem: Control accounts are prepared mainly to
options: check the arithmetical accuracy of the sales and purchases ledgers and help locate errors.
questions.explanation: A control account total should agree with the total of balances in the related ledger.

questions.stem: Sales ledger control: opening debit balance ₦420,000; credit sales ₦1,850,000; cash and cheques received ₦1,560,000; discount allowed ₦24,000; returns inwards ₦36,000; bad debts written off ₦10,000. The closing balance is
Which of the following appears on the credit side of a sales ledger control account?
questions.explanation: Receipts reduce amounts owed by customers, so they are credited.

questions.stem: A business made both cash and credit sales during March. Which of the following items will be left out of its sales ledger control account for March?
questions.explanation: Cash sales do not create debtors, so they never pass through the sales ledger.

questions.stem: Purchases ledger control: opening credit balance ₦310,000; credit purchases ₦1,240,000; payments to suppliers ₦1,105,000; discount received ₦18,000; returns outwards ₦27,000. The closing balance is
A customer who is also a supplier has his debt of ₦30,000 set off against the amount owed to him. The contra entry is
options: debit sales ledger control, credit purchases ledger control.
debit purchases ledger control, credit sales ledger control.
debit cash, credit sales ledger control.
questions.explanation: The set-off reduces both what customers owe (credit SLC) and what is owed to suppliers (debit PLC).

questions.stem: The credit sales figure in a sales ledger control account is obtained from the
questions.explanation: The total of the sales day book gives credit sales for the period.

questions.stem: A credit balance in a sales ledger control account most likely arises when
options: a customer has bought goods on credit.
a customer has overpaid or paid in advance.
discount is allowed to a customer.
questions.explanation: Overpayments or advances make the business owe the customer.

questions.stem: A customer's cheque of ₦45,000 is dishonoured by the bank. In the sales ledger control account, this is
questions.explanation: The customer again owes the amount, so receivables increase.

questions.stem: The sales ledger control balance is ₦640,000, but the list of individual customer balances totals ₦625,000. Which of the following could explain the difference?
options: A cash receipt of ₦15,000 was included in the control account but not posted to the customer's account.
Discount allowed of ₦15,000 was entered in the control account but not in the customer's account.
A sales invoice of ₦15,000 was completely omitted from the books.
A credit sale of ₦15,000 was entered in the sales day book but not posted to the customer's account.
questions.explanation: The control account includes the sale but the personal account does not, making the ledger total ₦15,000 lower.

questions.stem: Under a self-balancing ledger system,
options: all accounts are kept in one ledger.
each ledger has its own control (adjustment) account so that it can produce its own trial balance.
the cash book replaces the general ledger.
questions.explanation: Each ledger is made to balance independently through its control account.

questions.stem: Interest charged to a customer on an overdue account is recorded in the sales ledger control account on the
options: debit side of the purchases ledger control.
credit side of the purchases ledger control.
questions.explanation: Interest increases what the customer owes.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT appear in a purchases ledger control account?
questions.explanation: Allowances for doubtful debts relate to receivables and are never in the purchases ledger.

questions.stem: A statement listing the assets and liabilities of a business in order to find its capital, when proper books are not kept, is
questions.explanation: Capital = assets - liabilities, found from a statement of affairs.

questions.stem: Opening capital ₦450,000; closing capital ₦610,000; drawings ₦90,000; additional capital introduced ₦50,000. The profit for the year is

A major limitation of the single entry system is that
options: it is too expensive for small traders.
a trial balance cannot be prepared to check arithmetical accuracy.
questions.explanation: Without complete double entry, there is no trial balance and errors and fraud are hard to detect.

questions.stem: A receipts and payments account is
options: a statement showing the surplus or deficit of a club.
a statement of the club's assets and liabilities.
the same as an income and expenditure account.
a summary of the cash and bank transactions of a club for a period.
questions.explanation: It summarises actual receipts and payments, of both capital and revenue nature, without adjustments.

questions.stem: An excess of income over expenditure in an income and expenditure account is called
questions.explanation: Not-for-profit organisations use "surplus" and "deficit" instead of profit and loss.

questions.stem: A club received ₦380,000 in subscriptions during 2025. This included ₦20,000 owing for 2024 and ₦15,000 paid in advance for 2026. Subscriptions received in advance at the end of the year are shown in the statement of financial position of a club as
questions.explanation: The club owes members services for the following year.

questions.explanation: Assets 555,000 - liabilities 25,000 = ₦530,000.

questions.explanation: Depreciation is a non-cash expense; receipts and payments accounts record only cash flows.

questions.stem: Life membership fees received by a club are best treated by
options: crediting a life membership fund and transferring a fair portion to income each year.
treating the whole amount as income in the year received.
crediting it to the bar trading account.

3 marks: (b)(i) Relevance: information should influence users' economic decisions by helping them evaluate past, present or future events (predictive and confirmatory value), and be material and timely
2 marks: (b)(ii) Understandability: information should be presented clearly so that users with reasonable knowledge of business can understand it

(b) Relevant information is capable of making a difference to decisions through predictive or confirmatory value; understandable information is clearly classified and presented for users with reasonable knowledge.

questions.stem:
Explain the following accounting concepts, giving one example of the application of each:
(a) going concern; [3 marks]
(b) prudence; [3 marks]
(c) accruals; [3 marks]
(d) consistency; [3 marks]
(e) business entity. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) Going concern: the business is assumed to continue in operation for the foreseeable future (2); e.g. non-current assets valued at cost less depreciation rather than break-up value (1)
3 marks: (b) Prudence: profits are not anticipated but all foreseeable losses are provided for (2); e.g. inventory valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value / allowance for doubtful debts (1)
3 marks: (c) Accruals: revenue and expenses are recognised when earned or incurred, not when cash is received or paid, and matched in the same period (2); e.g. rent owing at year end added to rent paid (1)
3 marks: (d) Consistency: the same accounting methods are applied from one period to another unless there is good reason to change (2); e.g. using the same depreciation method every year (1)
3 marks: (e) Business entity: the business is treated as separate from its owner (2); e.g. owner's private expenses recorded as drawings, not business expenses (1)
questions.explanation: Going concern assumes continuity, so assets are carried at cost less depreciation. Prudence provides for losses but not unrealised gains, as in valuing inventory at the lower of cost and NRV. Accruals matches income and expenses to the period, as with accrued rent. Consistency requires the same methods each period, such as one depreciation method. Business entity separates owner and business, so private spending is drawings.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem:
The cash book of Kemi Ventures showed a debit bank balance of ₦286,500 on 31 March 2026, which did not agree with the bank statement. Investigation revealed the following:
(i) Cheques issued but not yet presented: No. 001 ₦45,000; No. 002 ₦18,200.
(ii) A lodgement of ₦62,000 made on 31 March had not been credited by the bank.
(iii) Bank charges of ₦2,300 appeared only on the bank statement.
(iv) A dividend of ₦25,000 was paid directly into the bank account by a company; it was not recorded in the cash book.
(v) A standing order of ₦15,000 for insurance premium had been paid by the bank but not entered in the cash book.
You are required to prepare:
(a) the adjusted cash book (bank column); [7 marks]
(b) the bank reconciliation statement as at 31 March 2026, showing the balance as per bank statement. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Balance b/d ₦286,500 and dividend received ₦25,000 on the debit side
3 marks: (a) Bank charges ₦2,300 and insurance standing order ₦15,000 on the credit side
2 marks: (a) Adjusted balance c/d ₦294,200
2 marks: (b) Start with balance as per adjusted cash book ₦294,200
3 marks: (b) Add unpresented cheques ₦63,200 (₦45,000 + ₦18,200)
2 marks: (b) Less uncredited lodgement ₦62,000
1 mark: (b) Balance as per bank statement ₦295,400
questions.explanation: (a) Adjusted cash book: 286,500 + 25,000 - 2,300 - 15,000 = ₦294,200 (debit). (b) Reconciliation: adjusted cash book 294,200 + unpresented cheques 63,200 - uncredited lodgement 62,000 = ₦295,400, the balance per bank statement.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between hire purchase and a credit sale. [6 marks]
(b) A machine with a cash price of ₦1,500,000 was bought on hire purchase on 1 January 2025 with a deposit of ₦300,000 and three annual instalments of ₦480,000 payable on 31 December each year. Calculate the total hire purchase interest. [3 marks]
(c) Allocate the interest to the three years using the sum-of-the-years'-digits method. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) Under hire purchase, ownership passes only when the last instalment is paid, whereas in a credit sale ownership passes immediately (2); under HP the seller can repossess the goods on default, whereas under a credit sale the seller can only sue for the debt (2); HP involves a deposit and instalments with interest, whereas credit sale may be a single deferred payment (2)
3 marks: (b) HP price = 300,000 + (3 x 480,000) = 1,740,000; interest = 1,740,000 - 1,500,000 = ₦240,000
6 marks: (c) Sum of digits 3 + 2 + 1 = 6: year 1 = 3/6 x 240,000 = ₦120,000; year 2 = 2/6 x 240,000 = ₦80,000; year 3 = 1/6 x 240,000 = ₦40,000 (2 marks each)
questions.explanation: (a) In hire purchase ownership passes on payment of the last instalment and the seller may repossess on default; in a credit sale ownership passes at once and the seller can only sue for payment. (b) Total payments 1,740,000 less cash price 1,500,000 = ₦240,000 interest. (c) Interest is front-loaded because the outstanding balance is highest early: ₦120,000, ₦80,000 and ₦40,000.

questions.stem:
(a) State five sources of revenue to the government of a West African country. [5 marks]
(b) Distinguish between capital expenditure and recurrent expenditure of government, giving two examples of each. [6 marks]
(c) State four differences between public sector accounting and private sector accounting. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) Any five, 1 mark each: taxes (personal income tax, company income tax, VAT); customs and excise duties; royalties and rents from mineral resources; fees, licences and fines; profits/dividends from public enterprises; grants and aids; loans/borrowing; sale of government property
3 marks: (b) Capital expenditure is spending on long-lasting assets that add to the productive capacity of the economy (1), e.g. construction of roads, building of schools/hospitals (2)
3 marks: (b) Recurrent expenditure is spending on day-to-day running of government that recurs every year (1), e.g. salaries of civil servants, maintenance, office supplies (2)
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: public sector is not profit-oriented while private sector aims at profit; public sector funds come from taxes and appropriation, private from owners and lenders; public sector emphasises accountability and compliance with appropriation laws; public sector is guided by the constitution and financial regulations, private by CAMA and accounting standards; public sector uses fund accounting and budgets as legal limits; ownership is the public versus private individuals
questions.explanation: (a) Governments earn revenue from taxes, customs and excise duties, mineral royalties, fees and fines, dividends from public enterprises, grants and borrowing. (b) Capital expenditure creates durable assets (roads, schools); recurrent expenditure covers day-to-day running costs (salaries, maintenance). (c) Public sector accounting is not profit-oriented, is financed by taxes and appropriations, stresses accountability and compliance with appropriation law and financial regulations, and uses fund accounting.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a financial system? [3 marks]
(b) State four differences between the money market and the capital market. [8 marks]
(c) Explain two methods by which a company can raise funds from the capital market. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) The set of financial institutions, markets, instruments and regulatory authorities through which funds are mobilised from savers and channelled to borrowers/investors
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: money market deals in short-term funds while capital market deals in long-term funds; money market instruments include treasury bills, commercial papers and call money while capital market instruments include shares, bonds and debentures; money market finances working capital while capital market finances long-term investment; money market is dominated by banks and the central bank while capital market involves stock exchanges, issuing houses and stockbrokers; money market is regulated mainly by the central bank while the capital market is regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission
4 marks: (c) Any two, 2 marks each: offer for subscription (company invites the public directly through a prospectus); offer for sale (shares sold through an issuing house to the public); rights issue (new shares offered to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings); private placement (shares sold to selected investors)
questions.explanation: (a) A financial system is the network of institutions, markets, instruments and regulators that mobilises savings and allocates them to investment. (b) The money market handles short-term funds and instruments such as treasury bills, is dominated by banks and supervised by the central bank; the capital market handles long-term funds such as shares and bonds and is regulated by SEC. (c) Companies raise capital through offers for subscription, offers for sale, rights issues and private placements.
